own_scenes.family: Hip hop, go-go y funk de los noventa
own_scenes.desc: Con la música negra popular muerta estéticamente, el alma del pueblo pasó al underground: un funk ruidoso, áspero y tenso, demasiado desesperado para la radio negra. Los breaks de DJ Kool Herc en las fiestas de barrio del Bronx, Jazzy Jay, Afrika Bambaataa, DJ Hollywood, Grandmaster Flash y Eddie Cheeba convirtieron la mezcla de discos en arte: los chavales dejaron las bandas por dos platos, el scratch y los breaks repetidos, un collage posmoderno de toda la música grabada sobre un ritmo funky. Sylvia Robinson grabó en 1979 «Rapper’s Delight» de la Sugarhill Gang y fichó a Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five, cuya «The Message» (1982), con Melle Mel, dio voz a los sin voz como no se oía desde «What’s Going On»; siguieron «White Lines» o «New York, New York». Las cajas de ritmos dieron un funk industrial y minimalista (el bombo 808, «Five Minutes of Funk» de Whodini), y Run-D.M.C. («It’s Like That», «Rock Box», «King of Rock», «Walk This Way» con Aerosmith en Raising Hell, 1986) asaltó la radio rock, seguidos por los Beastie Boys.

refs.q: With the aesthetic demise of black popular music, the soul of the people as it was expressed in the music went underground.
refs.para: With the aesthetic demise of black popular music, the soul of the people as it was expressed in the music went underground. The underground music of the eighties was generated by a new youth movement of deejays and emcees from every urban uptown, high-tech synthesizer wizards from around the world, and crafty old-school musicians all interpreting the impulse of The Funk. Eighties funk was a noisy, rugged, and tense interpretation of an African music and value system, fueled in part by the desperation of the inner cities. The monstrous, apocalyptic Hip Hop tracks of Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five featuring Melle Mel, the bone-crushing bass drum throbs and hysterical yelps of Run-D.M.C., and the relentlessly thick, funk grind of Trouble Funk’s live performances all reflected the intensity of eighties music—a music too desperate, too articulate, and too meaningful for so-called black radio.
refs.chapter: Cap. 20: Hip Hop and Black Noise: Raising Hell

refs.q: Once just the stage-setters, the presenters of music, Hip Hop deejays became the artists
refs.para: The New York Hip Hop scene is now a well-oiled legend, a mythic tale that has made its way into the pantheon of rock and roll folklore. The booming sounds and break mixes of DJ Kool Herc at midsummer Bronx block parties in the mid-seventies, the turntable wizardry of Jazzy Jay, Afrika Bambaataa, and DJ Hollywood at South Bronx disco clubs, and proto-rapping styles of Grandmaster Flash, DJ Hollywood, and Eddie Cheeba took mixing disco singles from a fad, to an art form, to a cultural symbol of resilience by the late 1970s. Youngsters in this environment abandoned their illusions of making music with bands, and instead lined up turntables and developed hyped mixing techniques such as the percussive record rotation known as scratching, the sound-strobe effect of transforming, and an ability to mix an endless supply of music onto synchronous, danceable beats. Adroit Hip Hop deejays could take the wickedest breakdowns of certain records—mixing them with identical copies—and repeat the breaks, sustaining a level of total hype. Craftier mixers rendered the entire history of recorded music into a scrap heap of the beat fragments at their disposal. Once just the stage-setters, the presenters of music, Hip Hop deejays became the artists as they took snippets of sounds, jingles, commercials, nursery rhymes, and pop standards and mixed them into a new, postmodern collage with a funky dance beat.
refs.chapter: Cap. 20: Hip Hop and Black Noise: Raising Hell

refs.q: As the voice of a forgotten social strata—poor black males from the inner city—Flash and his mates served a political function, by giving a voice to the voiceless.
refs.para: “The Message” was a window into the urban underworld that was never heard before on the radio—and unlike most rap records, it was heard on the radio. The despair, anger, and claustrophobia of life in the inner city was brought to the public uncut: “I can’t take the smell/I can’t take the noise/I got no money to move out/I guess I got no choice.” As the voice of a forgotten social strata—poor black males from the inner city—Flash and his mates served a political function, by giving a voice to the voiceless. Not since Marvin Gaye’s “What’s Goin’ On” in 1971 had social commentary been taken as seriously.

similar_scenes.name: Kurtis Blow y el primer rap de una multinacional
similar_scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
similar_scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
similar_scenes.desc: El periodista de Billboard Robert «Rocky» Ford, que intuyó el futuro del género, quiso con J. B. Moore un single navideño que volviera cada año; buscando artista dio con un joven promotor de fiestas de Queens, Russell Simmons, que le presentó a Kurtis Blow, b-boy convertido en MC que pinchaba en el Night Fever Disco de Hollis. «Christmas Rappin’» (1979), con Larry Smith al bajo y Denzil Miller a los teclados, entre James Brown y Chic, se pinchó hasta la primavera; Kurtis Blow fue el primer rapero fichado por una multinacional (Mercury) y «The Breaks» (1980) el primer disco de oro del hip hop. Simmons, que creía en los artistas como marcas en una época de discos de 12 pulgadas desechables, puso su foto en la portada. Kool Moe Dee: con Kurtis Blow aprendimos qué era un estribillo.
